analysis.one_liner: Bans stock brokers and investment advisers from forcing customers into arbitration and barring class-action lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Investor Choice Act, introduced with 11 House Democrats behind it, never left the House Financial Services Committee and died without a vote when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most brokerage and investment advisory contracts make customers sign away their right to sue in court, agree to arbitration in a forum the industry runs, and give up the right to join class actions. This bill would make those clauses illegal for brokers, dealers, and investment advisers, and would stop companies from forcing shareholders to arbitrate disputes through bylaws. It would void existing forced-arbitration clauses, except where arbitration had already started. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors — ordinary people with brokerage or retirement accounts — gain the choice to take disputes over fraud or bad advice to a judge or jury, to join a class action, and to pick their forum, instead of being locked into arbitration before an industry-selected arbitrator.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits broker-dealers and investment advisers from agreements that mandate arbitration, restrict forum choice, or bar customers from pursuing claims individually, as a class, or in a consolidated action [S3].
Voids prohibited provisions in agreements signed before enactment, unless arbitration had already been initiated by the enactment date [S3].

Bars companies from mandating arbitration of shareholder disputes in bylaws or shareholder agreements, and stops the SEC from registering, and exchanges from listing, securities of issuers with such requirements [S3].
The bill's findings state that mandatory arbitration clauses leverage brokers' power advantages to severely restrict defrauded investors' ability to seek redress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies lose the litigation shield that forced arbitration and class-action waivers provide; disputes would move to court, where outcomes can be larger, slower, and public. Some litigation costs may be passed to customers through fees.

drawbacks.text: Industry defenders argue FINRA arbitration is faster and cheaper for small investors than court, and that class actions often deliver little to individual class members while enriching plaintiffs' lawyers — so eliminating arbitration-by-default could raise costs without clearly improving recoveries for small claims [S3].
Opening brokerage disputes to court and class litigation could increase legal expenses, which firms may recover through higher account fees or by limiting services to small accounts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores a choice that most retail investors currently sign away without reading: the option to sue over fraud or misconduct. The cost is real but modest — more litigation for the industry and possibly slightly higher account costs — and the bill preserves voluntary arbitration for investors who prefer it. The strongest honest objection is that for small-dollar claims, arbitration may actually be more practical than court, but the bill's answer is that investors, not firms, should make that choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on December 6, 2019 by Rep. Bill Foster with 9 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and their industry-run arbitration system are better off: forced-arbitration and class-action waiver clauses remain fully enforceable, and investors still cannot take firms to court.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban forced arbitration in brokerage and advisory agreements

for.name: 10 of 231 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (including Reps. Maloney, Meeks, Casten, Lynch, Schakowsky, McGovern, Clay, Dean, and Heck)

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended

against.name: Brokerage and investment advisory industry
against.role: Firms whose customer contracts rely on mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers
against.what_they_did: Maintained the status quo in which the bill, which would have voided those clauses, died in committee without a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; the Financial Services Committee majority chose not to advance it to a vote.

industries.note: These firms require customers to sign agreements forcing disputes into arbitration before industry-run forums and waiving class-action rights, which sharply limits recovery for defrauded investors. The bill would have voided those clauses and opened firms to court suits.

Some issuers adopt bylaws forcing shareholder disputes into arbitration, which is widely seen as deterring shareholder lawsuits. The bill would have blocked registration and listing of securities by such issuers.

Mandatory customer arbitration currently channels disputes into a forum run by the securities industry; voluntary arbitration would remain available, but the default pipeline of compelled cases would end.
